faq.a: Yes; viral inflammation can block sinus drainage, allowing bacterial superinfection.
faq.q: Can a viral URI cause frontal sinusitis?

faq.a: When there is an abscess, bone erosion, or failure of medical therapy after 7–10 days.
High local resistance of Streptococcus pneumoniae and H. influenzae reduces efficacy.

exam: A patient with 5‑day frontal headache, fever, and tenderness over the brow presents; what is your immediate management plan? — Assess for complications, start oral amoxicillin‑clavulanate, advise saline irrigation, arrange CT if red flags develop.

How would you differentiate frontal sinusitis from migraine in a resource‑limited clinic? — Migraine lacks sinus tenderness, nasal discharge, and worsening on forward bending; sinusitis shows local tenderness and purulent discharge.

A chronic frontal sinusitis patient is HIV‑positive with weight loss; what additional investigations do you order? — Obtain sinus aspirate for GeneXpert/TB PCR and fungal microscopy; consider CT if available.

Why is intravenous ceftriaxone preferred for complicated frontal sinusitis? — Broad gram‑negative and gram‑positive coverage, good sinus penetration, and once‑daily dosing suitable for inpatient care.
What are the dangers of giving systemic steroids before confirming the aetiology? — Steroids can worsen undiagnosed TB or fungal infection, leading to dissemination.

Explain the pathophysiological link between obstruction of the ostiomeatal complex and sinusitis. — Obstruction traps secretions, creates a low‑oxygen environment, promotes bacterial overgrowth and mucosal inflammation.

When is surgical drainage indicated and what type is most feasible in low‑resource settings? — Indicated for abscess or failure of medical therapy; external frontal sinusotomy or bedside needle aspiration can be performed.
What red‑flag signs would prompt urgent referral to an ENT surgeon? — Visual loss, ophthalmoplegia, severe periorbital edema, neurological deficits, or signs of intracranial spread.
ai.title: Frontal Sinusitis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Inflammation of the frontal sinus often follows viral upper respiratory infection or bacterial superinfection. In low‑resource settings, TB and fungal causes are important. Recognise key history, exam, and pragmatic investigations to guide treatment.

b: Most common cause: viral URI with secondary bacterial overgrowth
Low‑resource tropics: consider Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Aspergillus spp., and fungal ball
Complications: orbital cellulitis, meningitis, epidural abscess
sections.p: Frontal sinusitis is inflammation of the frontal sinus cavity, usually secondary to obstruction of the ostiomeatal complex. It may be acute (<4 weeks), sub‑acute (4–12 weeks) or chronic (>12 weeks).

b: Acute: purulent discharge, frontal headache, fever, tenderness over frontal sinus
Chronic: persistent facial pressure, nasal obstruction, post‑nasal drip, possible mucopurulent discharge
Complicated: visual loss, ophthalmoplegia, neurological signs
sections.p: Diagnosis rests on a combination of symptom pattern, physical signs, and targeted investigations. Severity is staged by symptom duration and presence of complications.

b: History: recent URI, dental infection, trauma, exposure to dust or smoke, HIV status
Exam: frontal tenderness, swelling, possible periorbital edema, nasal mucosal edema, purulent discharge on endoscopy
Red flags: rapid visual loss, severe fever, neck stiffness
sections.p: Patients present to outpatient clinics or emergency wards with frontal headache that worsens on bending forward. In East Africa, co‑existing HIV or TB raises suspicion for atypical pathogens.

t.b: Is there air‑fluid level or opacification? Positive suggests sinus blockage; if unavailable, rely on clinical picture
What is the extent of mucosal thickening, bone erosion, or abscess? Confirms complications; if CT not available, treat empirically if red flags present
Which organism is present? Guides antibiotic choice; not essential for uncomplicated cases

t.a: TB PCR or GeneXpert on sinus aspirate
t.b: Is Mycobacterium tuberculosis present? Important in chronic cases with HIV or weight loss

b: First‑line oral antibiotics: amoxicillin‑clavulanate (covers common streptococci and H. influenzae); avoid macrolides if high resistance
If TB suspected: refer for anti‑TB therapy; avoid steroids until TB ruled out
Adjunctive saline nasal irrigation and topical decongestants to improve drainage
Severe or complicated cases: intravenous antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) and ENT referral for possible surgical drainage
sections.p: Treat the underlying infection, relieve obstruction, and monitor for complications. Use locally available antibiotics and supportive measures.

b: Migraine: usually unilateral, photophobia, no sinus tenderness
Orbital cellulitis: eyelid erythema, proptosis, limited eye movements
sections.p: Frontal sinusitis can mimic migraine, tension‑type headache, or orbital cellulitis.

b: A normal WBC does not rule out bacterial sinusitis in HIV patients
Negative culture does not exclude infection if antibiotics were started before sampling
sections.p: Normal plain X‑ray does not exclude early infection; CT is more sensitive. White blood cell count may be normal in early bacterial sinusitis or in immunocompromised patients.

b: Describe the stepwise approach to a patient with frontal headache and sinus tenderness
Explain why CT is preferred for suspected complications
State the rationale for choosing amoxicillin‑clavulanate over a macrolide
sections.p: Examiners test integration of history, exam, and pragmatic decision‑making, especially in resource‑limited settings.

b: Prescribing steroids before ruling out TB or fungal infection
Ordering MRI when CT is sufficient and more available
Ignoring HIV status when choosing antibiotics
sections.p: Typical pitfalls include over‑reliance on imaging, missing TB/fungal aetiology, and inappropriate steroid use.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of vision or eye movement
Severe periorbital swelling or bulging eye
